lead: A dual converter is two fully controlled bridges connected in inverse parallel to the same DC load. Converter P can pass current in one direction and converter N in the other, and each can make its voltage positive or negative with its firing angle, so the load can have either polarity of voltage and current: all four quadrants. Reversing DC drives for rolling mills, mine winders, lifts and crane hoists use it to drive, brake and reverse without switching contactors.
prereq: You need: fully controlled bridges with continuous current and inversion mode.

blocks.text: Converter P drives current +Id into the load; converter N, connected the other way round, drives −Id. With continuous current each gives an average voltage set by its own firing angle: for single-phase bridges V1 = (2Vm/π) cos α1 for P and, measured with the same load polarity, V2 = −(2Vm/π) cos α2 for N. For both to agree on the load voltage, V1 = V2, which needs
cos α1 = −cos α2   that is   α1 + α2 = 180°
blocks.where: α1 and α2 are the firing angles of P and N in degrees. When one bridge rectifies (α < 90°) the other is ready to invert (α > 90°).

blocks.text: The four quadrants are then: P rectifying (+V, +I, forward motoring); N inverting (+V, −I, forward braking, power returned); N rectifying (−V, −I, reverse motoring); P inverting (−V, +I, reverse braking). Some syllabi call the circuit a four-quadrant converter.

Equal average voltages are not equal instantaneous voltages: each bridge's output has a different ripple shape. If both bridges were gated with nothing between them, this ripple difference would drive a large current around the loop P–N, limited only by the source inductance.

items: Non-circulating mode: only one bridge receives gate pulses at a time. To reverse the current the controller removes the pulses of the conducting bridge, waits until its current has reached zero and its thyristors have recovered (a dead time of a few milliseconds), then releases the other bridge. No reactor is needed, but there is a short gap in torque.

Circulating-current mode: both bridges are gated all the time, with α1 + α2 = 180°, and an intergroup reactor between them limits the circulating current to a small fraction of the rated current. Each bridge carries its share of the circulating current plus the load current, so the current can change direction smoothly and quickly; the price is the reactor, larger thyristor ratings and extra losses.

blocks.text: In both modes the firing logic must never let both bridges conduct the load current with no reactor in the loop, which would short-circuit the supply through two thyristors.

A reversing rolling mill drives the metal one way, brakes, and drives it back, many times a minute. A crane hoist needs torque in the lifting direction both to lift a load and to lower a heavy one slowly (lowering it regeneratively, quadrant IV), and reverse torque only to drive a light hook down. Mine winders and lifts brake regeneratively on every trip. A single bridge with a reversing contactor is cheaper and is used where reversals are rare. Three-phase dual converters are the usual choice above a few kilowatts, and the same back-to-back bridges also make the two halves of a cycloconverter, met in the AC-AC converters topic.

examples.question: A single-phase dual converter feeds a 5 Ω resistance in series with a large inductance from 230 V, 50 Hz. Converter P is fired at α1 = 30°. Find V1 and the load current, and the angle α2 for converter N so that it is ready with the same voltage.
steps: The large inductance keeps the current continuous, so V1 = 207.07 × cos 30° = 179.33 V.
α2 = 180° − 30° = 150°. Converter N on its own gives 207.07 × cos 150° = −179.33 V, which, being connected the other way round, is +179.33 V at the load: the two agree.

examples.question: A three-phase dual converter on 415 V, 50 Hz supplies a DC motor with armature resistance 0.5 Ω. (a) Motoring at 50 A with back EMF E = 400 V: find α of converter P. (b) At the same speed (E still 400 V) the motor is braked at 50 A through converter N: find the terminal voltage, αN, and the power returned.
steps: (b) The current is now −50 A, so Vt = E + Id R = 400 − 25 = 375 V at the motor.
Converter N sees this voltage with reversed polarity: its own output must be −375 V, so cos αN = −375/560.45 = −0.6691 and αN = 132.0°. N is inverting.
Power returned to the supply = 375 × 50 = 18.75 kW. Check: the machine gives 400 × 50 = 20.0 kW and the armature loses 50² × 0.5 = 1.25 kW.

traps: Setting α2 = α1. The two bridges agree only when α1 + α2 = 180°.
Saying both bridges conduct in non-circulating mode. Only one gets gate pulses; the other waits through a dead time.
Thinking equal average voltages remove the circulating current. The ripple voltages differ, so the reactor is still needed.
Expecting αN below 90° in forward braking. N's own output must be negative (it inverts, αN > 90°) even though the motor's terminal voltage stays positive.

quiz.q: State the firing-angle condition for the two bridges of a dual converter.
quiz.a: α1 + α2 = 180°, so that cos α1 = −cos α2 and the average voltages match at the load.

quiz.q: Why is a dead time needed when a non-circulating dual converter reverses?
quiz.a: The outgoing bridge's current must fall to zero and its thyristors must recover their blocking ability before the other bridge fires; otherwise both conduct and short the supply.

quiz.q: A single-phase dual converter has Vm = 325 V and converter P at α1 = 60°. Find V1 and α2.
In non-circulating mode converter P supplies 35.9 A. What does converter N carry?
quiz.a: Nothing: N gets no gate pulses, so its current is zero.

quiz.q: Name the quadrant and the active bridge when a hoist lowers a heavy load slowly.
quiz.a: The speed is reversed but the torque stays in the lifting direction (same current direction as lifting), so the voltage is negative and the current positive: quadrant IV, with converter P inverting.

quiz.q: Compare circulating and non-circulating dual converters for a mill that reverses every few seconds.
quiz.a: Circulating mode has no dead time, so torque reverses smoothly and fastest, but it needs an intergroup reactor and carries extra current and losses. Non-circulating mode is cheaper and more efficient but leaves a few milliseconds without torque at each reversal. For frequent fast reversals the circulating mode is preferred.

quiz.q: What happens if the intergroup reactor saturates in circulating-current mode?
quiz.a: Its inductance collapses, so the ripple voltage drives a much larger circulating current through both bridges; the thyristors and reactor are overstressed and protection trips. The reactor is designed not to saturate at the peak circulating current.

beyond: Not for the exam. Four-quadrant DC drives are being replaced by AC drives with regenerative active front ends, but dual converters still run in old steel plants and in large mine winders. The same anti-parallel bridges make the cycloconverters of ship propulsion and cement mills. Search for 'four-quadrant DC drive', 'intergroup reactor design' and 'cycloconverter' next.

Right: the second worked example on the V–I plane: motoring through P at α1 = 40.7° (quadrant I) and braking at the same speed through N at αN = 132° (quadrant II).

spec.aria: Two thyristor bridges P and N fed from one three-phase supply. The positive terminal of P and the negative terminal of N are joined through two reactor halves, whose midpoint feeds the motor; the other motor terminal joins the remaining terminals of P and N. Beside them axes of terminal voltage against current with two points: 425 volts and plus 50 amperes, P rectifying at 40.7 degrees; 375 volts and minus 50 amperes, N inverting at 132 degrees; and labels for quadrants III and IV.
